common_name: Highway 290 Pink Buttons Rose (Found Texas Miniature Polyantha)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Highway 290 Pink Buttons is a 'found rose' discovered growing along the Texas highway for which it is named, prized as a tough, tiny-flowered polyantha for Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart for a low border or mass planting. Highway 290 Pink Buttons is a 'found rose' discovered growing wild along Highway 290 in Texas by rose rustlers and propagated under that descriptive name, bearing tiny, fully double, button-like pink pompon flowers in dense clusters nearly continuously from spring through fall. Its compact, twiggy, well-branched habit and diminutive flower size give it a dainty, old-fashioned charm well suited to edging, small borders, and containers. Like many found roses rescued from abandoned homesites, it is exceptionally tough and disease-resistant, needing no spray program even in humid Gulf South summers, and tolerates considerable heat and drought once established. Prune lightly in late winter to remove twiggy or dead growth.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Found Rose Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials
American Rose Society — Polyantha Class Descriptions

common_name: Grandmother's Hat Rose (Large Fragrant Found Bourbon-Type Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Grandmother's Hat is a large-flowered found rose of Bourbon-type parentage, named for the way its huge, ruffled blooms resemble an old-fashioned lady's hat.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to allow for its large, vigorous growth. Grandmother's Hat is a 'found rose' of Bourbon-type character, rescued and named by rose rustlers for its huge, ruffled, deeply fragrant pink blooms whose broad, layered petals were said to resemble an old-fashioned wide-brimmed lady's hat. It grows into a tall, vigorous shrub and repeat-blooms through the growing season with the same rich, classic old-rose fragrance prized in true Bourbon roses. Like other found roses rescued from old homesites, it is notably tough, disease-resistant, and tolerant of heat and neglect, needing little more than an occasional shaping prune in late winter to control its size.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Found Rose Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials

common_name: Cracker Rose (Found Florida Heritage Pink China-Type Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Cracker rose is a found heritage rose long grown around old Florida homesites, named for the 'cracker' pioneer culture of the region.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Cracker rose is a found heritage rose of China/Bourbon-type character, long grown and passed down around old homesites in Florida and named for the state's pioneer 'cracker' culture that preserved it outside the commercial nursery trade. It bears clusters of pink, semi-double, lightly fragrant flowers nearly continuously through the warm season on a vigorous, well-branched shrub adapted to the heat and humidity of the Deep South. Like other found roses rescued from long-abandoned homesites, it is notably tough and disease-resistant, needing no spray program and tolerating neglect, poor soil, and drought far better than modern hybrid roses. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Found Rose Collection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Heritage Rose Notes
